title: Spiritual Intention
speaker: Jeff Bickner
summary: Jeff Bickner's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating spiritual intention, which is motivation without attachment or grasping. This intention is directed towards bodhicitta, or the awakening to awareness with real clarity, and is crucial for spiritual practice. By setting an intention to approach ultimate truth with a genuine altruistic attitude, one can awaken to awareness in all aspects of life, not just during formal sitting practice, and embody the natural state of a bodhisattva.

There are so many Dharma events going on, and everything is so accessible nowadays through Zoom.
I'm really glad to have you here and that you came to listen to our speaker today.

So thank you very much, Jeff, for coming and giving a talk.
Thank you very much, Chris.
And hello to my old friend at Bellingham, Seishu, John Wiley.

I won't do that to you.
That was Koban.

The topic of my talk, though, is intention.
Not meeting others' expectations wasn't a stated intention.
It's just my observation of him during the five years I studied with him.
It was an opportunity for others to reflect on what just happened to them, or to awaken.
Expectations are another word for attachments or desires, the things that lead to suffering.
I'll give another example of Koban's way with expectations.
Back in 1971, *Zen and the Art of Archery* was first published.
There weren't a lot of books about Zen at the time, really.
And it was a big hit.
Koban was still teaching at Tassajara and San Francisco Zen Center.

It would change your life in a weekend.
It taught workshops, weekends.
What was missing was a workshop where one could see a Zen archer demonstrating the art of archery.
Koban was a master archer, and Baker Roshi insisted that Koban go down to Esalen and demonstrate for the folks down there.
Koban went down in full regalia with a six-foot-tall bow.
Esalen is situated on a cliffside with a big lawn next to a swimming pool.
The target was set up not very far from Koban, something like 50 feet.
Everyone gathered around with bated breath as Koban drew back the bow with perfect form, and then pivoted and shot the arrow out over the cliff and into the ocean, exclaiming, "Bullseye!"
No dog and pony show for Koban.
Look, some people's faces were priceless.
Reb Anderson also attended as a representative of Zen Center.
He later asked me if I thought Koban had broken the precepts.
I had to laugh.
Koban just wouldn't fulfill people's expectations like that.
Around 1980, Koban was thinking about moving to Taos.
I asked him point blank if he was moving to Taos, and he responded, "Nobody knows."
At that point, I moved to Santa Cruz from the Zen Center temple to a [unclear: "Ringgoltz"] farm, with a couple of practice periods at Tassajara thrown in.
In 1984, I married my wife, Jamie, and asked Koban to come up from Taos to do the ceremony.
He agreed.
I should have been nervous.
The day before the wedding, we had a rehearsal, so the doans would know exactly what to do and when to do it.
Big productions.
The next day, he totally ad libbed it.
He came off fine, except for some confused doans.
So that was Koban.
Everyone at Green Gulch loved Koban.
And he lived by example: you would see him, a Roshi, sweeping off the porch in front of his guest room.
No jisha serving him.
I want to bring this talk specifically back to the subject of spiritual intention, the nature of intention and expectations.
My full name that Norman gave me is Kisei Jishi, or Precious Vow, Compassionate Worker.
Until I received transmission, I was Kisei.
But now I am Jishi, Compassionate Worker.
Precious Vow was and is still my intention.
Norman used to tell people that I was someone who actually thought he could become a Bodhisattva.
I never claimed that.
But at a book signing about a year and a half ago, he told a crowd of 70 people that I am a Bodhisattva.
Well, I've been called worse things, I guess.
But I had to beg him never to do that again.
I said it just wouldn't do for me to develop hubris.
He agreed that that would be an unfortunate thing.
Nevertheless, it is my intention to be as wise and compassionate as possible, and it is not something I will ever finish.
But Precious Vow: we're talking about the Bodhisattva Vows.
I have formally taken them many times, and each time is deeper and more meaningful for me.
I took them at Jukai, then my wedding, my ordination as a priest, and my final transmission, and the retaking of my wedding vows with Norman after 20 years.
And my Shuso writes, when I first began my immersion in Buddhism, my intention was to wise up, to gain some measure of wisdom, and to stop being a jerk.
You can imagine, in my 20s, I was a jerk.
We all were.
By immersion, I thought I was going to throw myself in the stream of Buddhism and, like a gnarly rock, get some of the rough edges worn off.
I also kind of hoped to get enlightened.
But I didn't say much about that, as no one seemed to talk about getting enlightened.
And maybe that was just for Buddhas and Arhats.
In late 1998, I began practicing with my beloved teacher, Norman Fischer.
After a couple of months, Norman asked me to consider priesthood.
Now I really had to examine my intention seriously.
I concluded that I didn't want to throw up any roadblocks to my path.
So, in for a penny, in for a pound.
I didn't want to say I only want to go this far and no further.
I wanted the deepest experience of Buddhism I could have.
And so I returned to Tassajara with Norman in 1999.
I got to know the Bellingham and Vancouver sanghas, because Norman insisted I go wherever he taught for a number of years, something I figure was and is impractical for his other priests.
He warned me there was no curriculum vitae.
But this was going to be a Dharma transmitted Buddha to Buddha.
I consider myself incredibly lucky and grateful to have found this opportunity.
I encourage everyone to make an intention to study closely with your teachers.
For the past year, I have treated the pandemic as a long practice period.
Basically, I have been a hermit with my wife, never going out, because I'm at high risk, with a couple of episodes of pneumonia in the past four years.
So I've really enjoyed this opportunity.
I used to travel hither and yon visiting previous sangha members, friends and temples all over the world.
Now we Zoom all over the world.
My bride and I just finished a week-long retreat with Sokni Rinpoche in Nepal from our living room.
Very cool.
Some of you may have met Sokni Rinpoche when he was the resident teacher in Seattle at Bodhi Mandala.
A few years ago, we went to Seattle to do a workshop with him and fell in love with his style of teaching.
What is spiritual intention?
It can also be thought of as motivation, but not as a goal or a pursuit with grasping mind.
Actually, we might think of an intention to be non-dualistic, where subject and object merge into one.
I think this is the value of sesshin, where we get to dive deeply into our meditation and where our intention really matters.
Intentions and motivations can be honed in sesshin or anytime.
This reminds me of a Norman story.
This is from a sesshin in March of 1999 at Green Gulch Farm.
At the end of the sesshin, actually, we never knew when the last meditation period would be.
It was not announced.
But anyway, toward the end of the last day, we were sitting in the Green Gulch Zendo when I began to hear what I thought was a radio of some vehicle going down the road just outside the Zendo.
The volume kept rising until I could clearly hear it coming from inside the Zendo.
It was Norman playing a tape of Ella Fitzgerald singing "It Don't Mean a Thing If It Ain't Got That Swing."
That was something to think about, for sure.
What a way to end this sesshin.
So what was our experience?
And could we carry it forward?
Or was it just another "thank God it's Friday"?
I was recently listening to Sokni's first session of the retreat from Nepal.
He was speaking about intention.
I think these talks can be found at pundarika.org.
Anyway, he was conducting an exercise where we tried to locate our feeling of intention and drop it into our body, like taking a deep breath and letting it go with a big exhalation.
Here he is talking about intention as directed to bodhicitta, which can be thought of as a kind of altruistic feeling or the awakening to practice.
The intention of love, which he calls essence love, he is directing us to awakening to awareness that has real clarity.
He also uses what he calls handshake practice.
Handshake is taking whatever comes up as difficulty and shaking hands with it, staying with it until it dissolves.
His example is, if you're feeling frozen, acknowledge it and be with it.
Whatever arises is suchness.
It is our practice.
Everything we experience is suchness, and we reject nothing.
Handshake is not to fix anything.
It's just letting whatever it is resolve itself in an uncontrived way.
This is getting to transformation.
As Suzuki Roshi says, you should be able to appreciate things as an expression of big mind, which is always with you.
I'm going to read you some of what Sokni says about intention and motivation.
This is from his book, *Fearless Simplicity*.
If you can see that.

Okay.
*The real help here lies in continually correcting and improving our motivation, understanding why we are practicing and where we are ultimately heading.
Work on this and bring forth the noble motivation of bodhicitta.
Then all methods and practices can be used to help you progress in that direction.
Again, I must emphasize this point.
If we want to approach ultimate truth, we must form a true motivation.
This includes compassion for all other sentient beings who delude themselves continuously with the con with the contents of whatever arises in their minds.
Compassionate motivation says, how sad that they believe so strongly in their thoughts, that they take them to be so real.
This deluded belief in one's own thoughts is what I call the granddad concept.
First, we hold our thoughts as true.
Next, we accept that delusions and it becomes our granddad.
You know what it's like to suffer from this delusion yourself in your own experience.
Bring to mind all other sentient beings who let themselves get caught up in their granddad delusions and with compassion, form the wish to free them all.
That's the true motivation.
Please generate it.*
*Unless we have completely pure and true motivation, the practice of Vajrayana and Dzogchen doesn't turn out well.
Motivation is easy to talk about, yet sometimes hard to have.
We always forget the simplest things, partly because we don't take them seriously.
To really saturate yourself, your entire being with the Dharma, you need the proper motivation.
Please apply this thoroughly all the time.
In Vajrayana teachings, we find many instructions on how to improve our motivation.
In fact, you really learn about how this motivation should be.
The whole Bodhicitta teaching is contained within that.
Cultivate the correct motivation within your own experience and it turns into Bodhicitta all by itself.*
*I've been teaching now for 15 years to teach on the view on emptiness and so forth.

All of that is of course great, but when I look through the whole range of teachings, the real dividing line between whether one's practice goes in the right direction or the wrong direction always comes down to motivation.
That is the pivotal point.
Without pure motivation, no matter how profound the method is that we apply, it still turns out into spiritual materialism.
To train in being a bodhisattva and cultivate Bodhicitta so that I can be happy means something is twisted from the very beginning.
Instead, embrace your practice with a genuine Bodhicitta motivation and altruistic attitude.*
*Nyo Shokken Rinpoche, who was one of my gurus, would teach on motivation over and over again.
He talked about it so much that frankly I sometimes felt a little bored thinking, he talked about it yesterday, he talked about it today, and he will still probably talk about it tomorrow.
This is a little too much.
I've already heard it.
This kind of resistance is actually very good proof that ego doesn't like teachings on pure motivation.
Right there at that moment, one feels resistance against the altruistic attitude that is the precise spot to work with, touchy as it may be.
To admit this and be willing to deal with it right at that point is very practical, very pragmatic.
I think that the whole point of practice is using Dharma teachings at the exact point of resistance.
Otherwise, we just end up practicing when we feel good, and we avoid it when we feel bored or restless.
At that very moment of feeling depressed, restless, or unhappy, take these moods as a really good training opportunity, as a blessing, and put the Dharma to use right on the spot.
When we train in this type of welcoming practice on a daily basis, we can progress and become truly transformed.*
This welcoming practice is a basic Buddhist understanding.
We are present with whatever arises, and we don't put things off until we feel like we are ready to deal with whatever arises.
This is also one of the basic teachings of Lojong practice, which Norman writes about in his book, *Training in Compassion*.
I want to quote now from this book in regards to motivation.
Sorry, so much quotation.
Lojong practice is a Tibetan practice.
It's training the mind.
*Mind training begins, point one, resolve.
To begin with, our getting in touch with our deepest, best motivation.
As human beings, we are inherently motivated to see life truly and generously.
This is our human birthright.
Our human capacity is why every human community, from the dawn of time to the present, has some form of wholesome and salvific spiritual practice.
But the pressures of life and persistence of human folly embedded in these are in our societies and our communities, and therefore also in our own minds and hearts.
These have obscured this motivation in us.
So our course of training begins with getting up getting in touch with our best motivation.
I will note here what the reader will already have noticed, that mind training isn't a linear matter.
We don't fully complete one step and go on to the next.

We are constantly working on all the steps, partially completing one and then having to go back to it and all the others again, and again in circular fashion, which is why a review at this point is probably realistic.

Back to page two, then based on that sense of personal responsibility, training in the preliminaries involves reflecting on your life so that you can develop resolve, encourage to begin a new life, new life path.
Training in the preliminaries is the process of looking honestly at your life and making a firm decision to embark on a disciplined spiritual path.*
I'm gonna stop quoting Norman right now.

I won't burden you with that yet.
Several years ago, Norman asked me to teach Lojong in the Everyday Zen seminar.
I had no idea what it was.
He gave me some books to read, even though there's no curriculum to take.
So this was before he wrote the book.
Lojong has some 50 sayings, or more actually.
The book he has written is called *Training in Compassion*, Zen teachings on the practice of Lojong.
Anyway, Lojong has some 50-plus sayings or considerations that you work with, consider and perhaps even journal about.
I have these 50 some sayings all prepared in a form that I can email to anybody who wants them.
You just cut them out and put them one by one on your refrigerator, day to day, or on the mirror or whatever.
If you want to email me, just email me at jbickner at earthlink.net.
I'll do it soon, because I'm going to change that email.
So we have our overarching intention or motivation.
Of course, we have moment-by-moment intentions.
But our overarching intention is like the Bodhisattva precepts.
These precepts are the description of the way a Bodhisattva is, just naturally is.
As Suzuki Roshi says, "When you observe the precepts without trying to observe the precepts, that is true observation of the precepts."
Thank you.
Since the topic for you at this period of time is enlightenment, or awakening, I will say that awakening can arise at any moment, and usually not on the cushion.
I think sitting on the cushion prepares us for awakening.
I've talked to quite a few people who have had awakening experiences, and none of them was on the cushion.
Even Dogen was awakened by the sound of Rujing's voice, telling someone next to him to drop off body and mind.
So since you can awaken anytime, if not now, when?
Thank you very much.
Do we have time for questions?
Okay, I'll take any questions.
Just raise your hand.
I'll see you.
